comments.text:
I've noticed that politicians seem to think AI can do things that it cannot. For example, Virginia's Governor Youngkin was waving around a bundle of papers saying that AI had consolidated bureaucratic red tape. Implicit in this claim was the perception that AI had reviewed tomes of laws and regulations and whatnot  to eliminate redundancy. 

We know LLMs cannot do this. At the same time, we know that LLMs will cheerfully produce documents that claim to do this, but really just lose coherence and wind up transcribing lorem Ipsum instead.

Politicians don't understand that AI loses the plot like this. There appears to be an incredible disconnect between what AIs do and what politicians believe that they do. At the same time, governments are throwing vast amounts of capital at AI, not just at the big boys, but at hastily created fly-by-night outfits that are really just gaining access to sensitive data and feeding prompts to some big boy's API.

That shit needs to stop.

comments.author: @UFPharmacy
comments.text: Some of the language in this document is a bit concerning. In particular, the part about the government only contracting with LLM developers who ensure that their systems are objective and free from top-down ideological bias. Let's be clear about what this language actually means coming from this administration. "Objective and free from top-down ideological bias" should be seen as nothing more than thinly veiled code for AI that is forced to align with their political narrative. This is less about AI policy and more about controlling the future of information. The end goal would be to effectively redefine 'objective' to mean 'agrees with us,' while labeling any established scientific or academic consensus ('top down) that contradicts them as 'ideological bias.' They're laying the groundwork to define "truth" by government contract here. Given this administration's track record with facts and information, this should be seen not as an objective search for neutrality, but a strategic move to use the power of federal contracts to compel tech companies into building an information ecosystem that validates their worldview, effectively turning AI into a tool for institutionalizing their own version of the truth.

comments.author: @DerekBodily
comments.text: I think America is losing the race, but doesn't realize it. We're significantly behind on multiple fronts, while China is only behind on one. That front is creating the "software" behind AGI, but that is the thing everybody is trying to figure out, and China's really not that far behind. I also think their approach is correct, in that they're focusing on open source, while the US has a dozen companies burning through billions to create AI that will probably be worth nothing because it will end up being the same quality as something free. Just like Apple overtook Microsoft by making the software free. Manufacturing and energy production are much bigger concerns because they both require a massive amount of resources - both human and material. So while we have a massive amount of people chipping away at the AGI problem, we need even more people building nuclear power plants to at least double our power output. Then comes manufacturing. If we can't make the robots and devices that will bring AGI to life, we're going to lose. End of story. And bringing that much manufacturing power online in less than a decade is going to be nearly impossible considering we're basically starting at zero. While those are huge hurdles to clear, I think the biggest hurdle is the human talent required to make this happen. The brain rot has spread so far and wide in American culture that it's going to be hard to get the right people trained up to fill the roles needed to create this energy and manufacturing capacity.
